The attack failed. I downloaded the Mitchell translation in full (Gutenberg pg26163.txt, 868,932 bytes) to the scratchpad and read the sentence in place rather than accepting the verifier's account of it. At line 523 the text runs: 'Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.' That is the proposed quotation exactly, and it is a complete sentence in the edition, not a clause lifted out of a longer one — which was my first line of attack, since 'gnaws into the future' has the shape of a fragment that anthologies like to strand.

TRANSLATOR CONFIRMED AT THE SOURCE. The file header gives 'Title: Creative Evolution', 'Author: Henri Bergson', 'Translator: Arthur Mitchell'. The 1911 Henry Holt date is standard for Mitchell. Drift was the danger worth chasing, because duree is the most contested noun in Bergson and later translators handle 'ronge' differently; the proposal carries Mitchell's 'gnaws into', which is the wording the source line claims. Right text, right credit.

LOCATOR CONFIRMED BY BRACKETING. 'Chapter I' is only true if the sentence falls before chapter II, and a chapter claim is cheap to make and easy to get wrong. I grepped the chapter heads: the body's CHAPTER I is at line 417 and CHAPTER II at line 3308 (the four earlier hits at 115 to 184 are the table of contents). The sentence at 523 is about a hundred lines into chapter I. Locator holds. The context the verifier described also holds word for word: it follows 'our duration is not merely one instant replacing another; if it were, there would never be anything but the present' and is followed within two sentences by 'Memory, as we have tried to prove, is not a faculty of putting away recollections in a drawer'. That is the passage, not a lookalike elsewhere in the book — and there is a lookalike, at line 1679, 'that duration which gnaws on things, and leaves on them the mark of its tooth', which I checked precisely because a verifier who had only grepped for 'gnaw' could have landed on the wrong one. The proposal has the right occurrence.

A STRONGER LOCATOR EXISTS BUT I AM NOT PUTTING IT IN betterCitation. The Mitchell edition's own index (under Duration) lists 'gnawing of, 4, 8, 46', so this first occurrence is almost certainly p. 4 of the 1911 Holt printing, and a page would be tighter than a chapter for a chapter that runs some seventy pages. I am leaving betterCitation empty on purpose: the Gutenberg text carries no page breaks, so p. 4 is inferred from the index and my own count, not read off a page image, and this track's standard is that nothing gets minted. If the editor wants the page, someone should confirm it against a scan of the Holt printing first; 'chapter I' as proposed is honest and correct as it stands and ships safely.

THEME AND SIX A.M. This is the best thematic fit of the four for an August of impermanence: it is the line that refuses to treat passing as loss, since for Bergson the past is not what is gone but what swells. Nothing bleak, nothing graphic, nothing needing a warning.

THE ONE REAL WEAKNESS, WHICH IS NOT A CITATION FAULT. 'Gnaws into the future' is a hard image cold at six in the morning, and an empty note leaves the reader to work out that duration here means lived time rather than clock time. The month can carry it, but of the four this is the line most improved by a short note.
